text:
[latex] A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, [/latex]
then which ONE of the following is [latex]A^8 [/latex]?
solution:
Eigenvalues of [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex]: [latex](1-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)-4=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2-1-4=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2=5\Rightarrow\lambda=\pm\sqrt5[/latex]

Since [latex]A[/latex] is symmetric, it's diagonalizable with these eigenvalues, and [latex]A^8[/latex] has eigenvalues [latex](\sqrt5)^8=5^4=625[/latex] and [latex](-\sqrt5)^8=625[/latex] as well (both eigenvalues raised to an even power give the same positive result). Since both eigenvalues of [latex]A^8[/latex] equal [latex]625[/latex], [latex]A^8[/latex] is simply the scalar matrix [latex]625I[/latex].

Answer: [[625,0],[0,625]]

text:
The value of [latex]x [/latex] such that [latex]x > 1 [/latex], satisfying the equation
[latex]  \int_{1}^{x}t \ln t \, dt = \frac{1}{4} [/latex] is
solution:
Integrate by parts: with [latex]u=\ln t,\ dv=t\,dt[/latex] (so [latex]du=dt/t,\ v=t^2/2[/latex]):
[latex]\int t\ln t\,dt=\dfrac{t^2}2\ln t-\int\dfrac{t}2\,dt=\dfrac{t^2}2\ln t-\dfrac{t^2}4[/latex]

Evaluating from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]x[/latex]: [latex]\left(\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4\right)-\left(0-\dfrac14\right)=\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4+\dfrac14[/latex]

Setting this equal to [latex]\dfrac14[/latex]: [latex]\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4=0\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{x^2}2\left(\ln x-\dfrac12\right)=0[/latex]
Since [latex]x>1[/latex] means [latex]x^2\ne0[/latex], we need [latex]\ln x=\dfrac12\ \Rightarrow\ x=e^{1/2}=\sqrt e[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\sqrt{e}[/latex]

text:
Consider a binary tree [latex]T [/latex] in which every node has either zero or two children. Let [latex]n > 0 [/latex] be the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex].
Which ONE of the following is the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex] that have exactly two children?
solution:
In a binary tree where every node has [latex]0[/latex] or [latex]2[/latex] children, let [latex]I[/latex] be the number of [latex]2[/latex]-children (internal) nodes and [latex]L[/latex] the number of leaves. A basic counting fact for such trees: [latex]L=I+1[/latex] (each internal node, when added, net-increases the leaf count by exactly one over what it replaced).

Total nodes: [latex]n=I+L=I+(I+1)=2I+1\ \Rightarrow\ I=\dfrac{n-1}2[/latex]

Answer: (n-1)/2

Let [latex]L [/latex], [latex]M [/latex], and [latex]N [/latex] be non-singular matrices of order 3 satisfying the equations

[latex] L^2 = L^{-1}, \quad M = L^8, \quad N = L^2. [/latex]

Which ONE of the following is the value of the determinant of [latex](M - N) [/latex]?
solution:
From [latex]L^2=L^{-1}[/latex], multiply both sides by [latex]L[/latex]: [latex]L^3=L^2\cdot L=L^{-1}\cdot L=I[/latex]. So [latex]L[/latex] has order dividing [latex]3[/latex].

[latex]M=L^8=L^{6+2}=(L^3)^2\cdot L^2=I^2\cdot L^2=L^2[/latex]. But we're also given [latex]N=L^2[/latex]. So [latex]M=N[/latex] exactly, meaning [latex]M-N[/latex] is the zero matrix.

[latex]\det(M-N)=\det(0)=0[/latex]

Answer: 0

text: Let [latex]P(x) [/latex] be an arbitrary predicate over the domain of natural numbers. Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?
solution:
This is exactly the statement of the principle of mathematical induction: if a predicate [latex]P[/latex] holds for the base case [latex]0[/latex], and truth of [latex]P(x)[/latex] always guarantees truth of [latex]P(x+1)[/latex] (the inductive step, moving forward), then [latex]P[/latex] holds for every natural number.

The other options either use a backward step ([latex]P(x)\Rightarrow P(x-1)[/latex], which can't reach numbers larger than the base case) or start from a base case like [latex]1000[/latex] (which, even with a valid forward or backward step, can never establish [latex]P[/latex] for numbers below [latex]1000[/latex] using only a one-directional step) — none of these actually guarantee [latex]P[/latex] for every natural number.

Answer: (P(0) ∧ (∀x[P(x)⇒P(x+1)])) ⇒ (∀x P(x))

text:
Consider the following statements:

(i) Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address.
(ii) A single TCP segment from a sender S to a receiver R cannot carry both data from S to R and acknowledgement for a segment from R to S.

Which ONE of the following is CORRECT?
solution:
(i) ARP maps IP addresses to hardware (MAC) addresses: this is exactly ARP's definition — TRUE.

(ii) "A single TCP segment cannot carry both data and an acknowledgement": this is FALSE. TCP is full-duplex, and a very common optimization called piggybacking lets a single outgoing segment simultaneously carry new data (from S to R) and an acknowledgement field (ACKing previously received data from R) — the TCP header always has an ACK field available regardless of whether the segment also carries data.

Answer: (i) is TRUE and (ii) is FALSE

text:
A machine receives an IPv4 datagram. The protocol field of the IPv4 header has the protocol number of a protocol X.
Which ONE of the following is NOT a possible candidate for X?
solution:
The IPv4 protocol field identifies which higher-layer protocol's data the datagram carries, using standard registered numbers: ICMP [latex]=1[/latex], IGMP [latex]=2[/latex], OSPF [latex]=89[/latex] — all of these run directly over IP and have their own dedicated protocol number.

RIP, however, is not carried directly over IP; it runs as an application-layer protocol on top of UDP (using UDP port [latex]520[/latex]). So an IP datagram carrying RIP traffic would have its protocol field set to UDP's number ([latex]17[/latex]), never a dedicated "RIP" protocol number.

Answer: Routing Information Protocol (RIP)

text:
Consider an unordered list of [latex]N [/latex] distinct integers.
What is the minimum number of element comparisons required to find an integer in the list that is NOT the largest in the list?
solution:
We just need to find some element guaranteed not to be the overall largest — not identify the largest itself, and not verify anything about the rest of the list.

Compare any two elements of the list against each other: whichever of the two is smaller is guaranteed to not be the maximum of the whole list (since the larger of this pair beats it, so it can't possibly be the overall largest). This requires only one comparison, and works for any list of [latex]N\ge2[/latex] distinct integers.

Answer: 1

text:
Given the following syntax-directed translation rules:

[latex] \text{Rule 1: } R \rightarrow AB \{ B.i = R.i - 1; A.i = B.i; R.i = A.i + 1; \} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Rule 2: } P \rightarrow CD \{ P.i = C.i + D.i; D.i = C.i + 2; \} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Rule 3: } Q \rightarrow EF \{ Q.i = E.i + F.i; \} [/latex]

Which ONE is the CORRECT option among the following?
solution:
Classify each rule by whether it uses only synthesized attributes (S-attributed: every attribute is computed purely from children) versus whether it's L-attributed (inherited attributes may only depend on the parent or strictly-left siblings, evaluated left to right):

Rule 1 ([latex]R\to AB\{B.i=R.i-1;\ A.i=B.i;\ R.i=A.i+1;\}[/latex]): [latex]A.i[/latex] is defined using [latex]B.i[/latex] — but [latex]B[/latex] is to the right of [latex]A[/latex] in the production, so this inherited-attribute dependency flows backward (right-to-left), violating L-attributed rules. It's also not S-attributed, since [latex]B.i[/latex] is set from [latex]R.i[/latex] (an inherited attribute from the parent). Neither S-attributed nor L-attributed.

Rule 2 ([latex]P\to CD\{P.i=C.i+D.i;\ D.i=C.i+2;\}[/latex]): [latex]D.i[/latex] (inherited) is set using only [latex]C.i[/latex], a left sibling — perfectly valid for L-attributed. But since [latex]D[/latex] does have an inherited attribute at all, the SDT is not purely synthesized. Not S-attributed, but is L-attributed.

Rule 3 ([latex]Q\to EF\{Q.i=E.i+F.i;\}[/latex]): the only attribute defined is [latex]Q.i[/latex], computed purely from its children [latex]E,F[/latex] — purely synthesized. S-attributed (and therefore also L-attributed, since S-attributed is a special case of L-attributed).

Answer: Rule 1 is neither; Rule 2 is not S-attributed but is L-attributed; Rule 3 is both S-attributed and L-attributed.

text:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1500 bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes.
Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header?
solution:
Ethernet frame data field max [latex]=1500[/latex] bytes; IPv4 header [latex]=20[/latex] bytes (no options), so max IP data per fragment [latex]=1500-20=1480[/latex] bytes — conveniently already a multiple of [latex]8[/latex], so no further rounding needed.

The UDP segment (header [latex]8[/latex] bytes [latex]+[/latex] payload [latex]7488[/latex] bytes [latex]=7496[/latex] bytes) becomes the IP datagram's data, which must be fragmented:
[latex]7496\div1480=5.06\ldots[/latex], so [latex]5[/latex] full fragments of [latex]1480[/latex] bytes ([latex]7400[/latex] bytes) plus a final fragment of [latex]7496-7400=96[/latex] bytes of data.

Total fragments [latex]=5+1=6[/latex]. Last fragment's total size (including its own [latex]20[/latex]-byte IP header) [latex]=96+20=116[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 6 fragments, 116 bytes

text: Which ONE of the following languages is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton?
solution:
A deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) accepts exactly the class of deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs), which is a proper subset of all context-free languages — some CFLs (like certain languages requiring "guessing" where a string's midpoint is) are inherently non-deterministic and can never be accepted by any DPDA, only by a general (non-deterministic) PDA.

Since every regular language can always be recognized by a DFA (which is trivially also a valid DPDA that simply never uses its stack), every regular language is guaranteed accepted by some DPDA.

"Any context-free language," "any NPDA-accepted language" (these are the same, broader class, and DPDA is a strictly weaker/smaller class), and "any decidable language" (a vastly larger class, including languages that aren't even context-free) are all too broad to be guaranteed DPDA-acceptable.

Answer: Any regular language.

text:
Let [latex]G_1, G_2 [/latex] be Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) and [latex]R [/latex] be a regular expression. For a grammar [latex]G [/latex], let [latex]L(G) [/latex] denote the language generated by [latex]G [/latex].
Which ONE among the following questions is decidable?
solution:
Checking the decidability of each question about context-free grammars:

- Is [latex]L(G_1)=L(G_2)[/latex]? Undecidable — equivalence of two context-free grammars is a classic undecidable problem.
- Is [latex]L(G_1)\cap L(G_2)=\emptyset[/latex]? Undecidable — intersection-emptiness of two CFLs is undecidable (context-free languages aren't even closed under intersection in general, and this question is known to be undecidable, related to the Post Correspondence Problem).
- Is [latex]L(G_1)=L(R)[/latex]? (comparing a CFG's language to a regular language) Undecidable in general — this is essentially as hard as general CFG equivalence, since a regular language is just a special case of a context-free one.
- Is [latex]L(G_1)=\emptyset[/latex]? Decidable! Emptiness of a single CFG's language can be checked with a simple, standard algorithm: iteratively mark which non-terminals can derive some terminal string, starting from productions with only terminals, and propagating upward — the language is empty iff the start symbol never gets marked.

Answer: Is L(G1) = ∅? (this is the only decidable one)

text:
An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account [latex]A [/latex] attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. 10000 each from account [latex]A [/latex] to account [latex]B [/latex]. Both transactions read the same value, Rs. 11000, as the initial balance in [latex]A [/latex] and were allowed to go through. [latex]B [/latex] was credited Rs. 10000 twice. [latex]A [/latex] was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. 1000.
Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system?
solution:
This is a classic lost-update anomaly caused by two transactions reading the same stale value and overwriting each other's effects.

- Consistency is violated: the database ends up in a state that breaks the intended invariant (money should be conserved / correctly transferred), since [latex]A[/latex] should have ended up [latex]11000-20000[/latex] worth adjusted correctly but instead only one debit actually applied while both credits landed — the books don't balance as intended.
- Isolation is violated: the two concurrent transactions were not properly isolated from each other — both read [latex]A[/latex]'s balance before either had committed its update, letting their effects clash (textbook lost-update problem).
- Atomicity is not necessarily violated: each individual transaction ran to completion in full (no partial execution of a single transaction occurred).
- Durability is unrelated here: there's no indication of any committed-then-lost data due to a crash.

Answer: Consistency and Isolation

text: Which of the following is/are part of an Instruction Set Architecture of a processor?
solution:
The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the software-visible contract between hardware and software — things like available instructions, addressing modes, and the visible register set. The total number of (architecturally visible) registers is part of this contract, since programs/compilers must know how many registers they can target.

Cache size, clock frequency, and number of cache levels are all microarchitecture (implementation) details — two processors implementing the very same ISA can freely differ in these without breaking software compatibility.

Answer: The total number of registers

text: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph [latex]G [/latex] is/are TRUE?
solution:
Checking each BFS/DFS claim on an undirected simple graph:

- "A DFS tree is a shortest path tree": false — DFS explores as deep as possible along one branch first and gives no shortest-path guarantee at all; only BFS guarantees that.
- "Every non-tree edge w.r.t. a DFS tree is a forward/back edge": true — in an undirected graph, DFS can never produce a cross edge; every non-tree edge necessarily connects an ancestor-descendant pair (classified as a back edge, viewable from either endpoint as forward/back).
- "Non-tree BFS edge (u,v): distances differ by at most 1": true — this is a standard BFS property, since BFS explores level-by-level and any edge can only connect vertices in the same level or adjacent levels.
- "Both BFS and DFS can find connected components": true — running either traversal repeatedly from every yet-unvisited vertex correctly partitions the graph into its connected components.

Answer: The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th statements are all true.

Consider the two lists List I and List II given below:
[latex] \begin{array}{|c l|c l|} \hline \textbf{List I} & & \textbf{List II} & \\ \hline \text{(i)} & \text{Context free languages} & \text{(a)} & \text{Closed under union} \\ \hline \text{(ii)} & \text{Recursive languages} & \text{(b)} & \text{Not closed under complementation} \\ \hline \text{(iii)} & \text{Regular languages} & \text{(c)} & \text{Closed under intersection} \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
solution:
Recall the closure properties: Context-free languages are closed under union, but famously not closed under complementation (matching (i)-(b)) and also not closed under intersection in general. Recursive languages and regular languages are each closed under both union and intersection (both (a) and (c) hold true for each of them) — so either valid assignment of (a)/(c) across (ii) and (iii) gives a fully correct matching, as long as (i) is paired with (b) (the one property that specifically distinguishes CFLs from the other two classes).

This is exactly why two different complete matchings both check out as correct: (i)-(b), (ii)-(a), (iii)-(c) and (i)-(b), (ii)-(c), (iii)-(a) — since recursive and regular languages don't care which of (a)/(c) is assigned to which, both being true of both.

Answer: (i)-(b),(ii)-(a),(iii)-(c) AND (i)-(b),(ii)-(c),(iii)-(a)

text:
Consider the following logic circuit diagram.

Which is/are the CORRECT option(s) for the output function [latex]F [/latex]?
solution:
From the given circuit: a NAND gate takes inputs [latex]X,Y[/latex] directly, giving [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex]; a separate inverter taps the [latex]X[/latex] line alone, giving [latex]\bar X[/latex]; and a third branch inverts [latex]Y[/latex] then ANDs it with [latex]X[/latex], giving [latex]X\bar Y[/latex]. All three signals feed into a final OR gate:

[latex]F=\overline{XY}+\bar X+X\bar Y[/latex]

By De Morgan's law, [latex]\overline{XY}=\bar X+\bar Y[/latex], so this simplifies to [latex]F=\bar X+\bar Y+X\bar Y[/latex]. But the term [latex]X\bar Y[/latex] is already fully covered/absorbed by [latex]\bar Y[/latex] alone (whenever [latex]X\bar Y[/latex] is true, [latex]\bar Y[/latex] is automatically true too) — so by the absorption law, [latex]F=\bar X+\bar Y[/latex] exactly, which is the same function as [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex] itself.

So [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex], [latex]\bar X+\bar Y+X\bar Y[/latex], and [latex]\overline{XY}+\bar X+X\bar Y[/latex] are all just different (redundant) ways of writing the exact same underlying function; only [latex]X+\bar Y[/latex] is a genuinely different function.

Answer: [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex]; [latex]\bar X+\bar Y+X\bar Y[/latex]; and [latex]\overline{XY}+\bar X+X\bar Y[/latex] (all equivalent, all correct).

Adding the same positive constant [latex]\alpha[/latex] to every edge shifts the total weight of any spanning tree by exactly [latex]\alpha\times(n-1)[/latex] (since every spanning tree has exactly [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, the same count) — a uniform shift that doesn't change which spanning tree has the minimum total weight. An array [latex]A [/latex] of length [latex]n [/latex] with distinct elements is said to be bitonic if there is an index [latex]1 \leq i \leq n [/latex] such that [latex]A[1..i] [/latex] is sorted in the non-decreasing order and [latex]A[i+1..n] [/latex] is sorted in the non-increasing order.
Which ONE of the following represents the best possible asymptotic bound for the worst-case number of comparisons by an algorithm that searches for an element in a bitonic array [latex]A [/latex]?
solution:
A bitonic array first increases then decreases (or vice versa). At any index, comparing the current element to its neighbors tells you which "half" (increasing or decreasing) you're in, and binary search can be adapted to search each half:

First locate the peak (maximum) element using a binary-search-style approach in [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex] (comparing an element to its neighbors to decide which direction has the larger values). Once the peak is found, the array splits into two ordinary sorted sequences (one increasing, one decreasing), and each can be searched with ordinary binary search, also [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex].

Combining these steps keeps the total worst-case comparisons at [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex], matching what you'd get for a single sorted array — no better bound like [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex] is achievable (you must still narrow down the location), and no worse bound like [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] or [latex]\Theta(\log^2n)[/latex] is necessary.

Answer: Θ(log n)

[latex] \forall f, g \in \mathcal{F}, \, f \preceq g \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \forall x \in \{1, \dots, n\}, f(x) \leq g(x), \text{ where } 0 \leq 1. [/latex]
Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
solution:
[latex]f\preceq g[/latex] iff [latex]f(x)\le g(x)[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex] — this is the standard pointwise "less than or equal to" ordering on binary functions.

- Reflexive: [latex]f(x)\le f(x)[/latex] always. Antisymmetric: if [latex]f\preceq g[/latex] and [latex]g\preceq f[/latex], then [latex]f(x)=g(x)[/latex] for all [latex]x[/latex], so [latex]f=g[/latex]. Transitive: chains through in the obvious way. So [latex]\preceq[/latex] is a genuine partial order (not symmetric, and not an equivalence relation, since e.g. [latex]f\preceq g[/latex] doesn't imply [latex]g\preceq f[/latex] unless [latex]f=g[/latex]).

- Lattice: for any two functions [latex]f,g[/latex], their pointwise max (taking [latex]\max(f(x),g(x))[/latex] at every [latex]x[/latex]) is their least upper bound, and their pointwise min is their greatest lower bound — both always exist within [latex]\mathcal F[/latex]. So [latex](\mathcal F,\preceq)[/latex] is indeed a lattice.

Answer: (F,⪯) is a partial order; and (F,⪯) is a lattice.

[latex] L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ l_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ l_{31} & l_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad U = \begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12} & u_{13} \\ 0 & u_{22} & u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & u_{33} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

Solving via [latex]LY=Q[/latex] then [latex]UX=Y[/latex]: substituting [latex]P=LU[/latex] into [latex]PX=Q[/latex] gives [latex]L(UX)=Q[/latex]; setting [latex]Y=UX[/latex], we solve [latex]LY=Q[/latex] first (easy, forward substitution since [latex]L[/latex] is lower triangular), then [latex]UX=Y[/latex] (easy, back substitution). If [latex]P[/latex] is invertible, both [latex]L,U[/latex] invertible: [latex]L[/latex] is unit lower-triangular (diagonal all [latex]1[/latex]s), so [latex]\det(L)=1[/latex] always, regardless of [latex]P[/latex] — [latex]L[/latex] is always invertible. Since [latex]\det(P)=\det(L)\det(U)=\det(U)[/latex], if [latex]P[/latex] is invertible ([latex]\det(P)\ne0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)\ne0[/latex] too. True.

If [latex]P[/latex] singular, some diagonal element of [latex]U[/latex] is zero: since [latex]\det(P)=\det(U)[/latex] (product of [latex]U[/latex]'s diagonal, as [latex]U[/latex] is upper triangular), if [latex]P[/latex] is singular ([latex]\det(P)=0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)=0[/latex], which for a triangular matrix forces at least one diagonal entry to be [latex]0[/latex]. True.

If [latex]P[/latex] symmetric, both [latex]L,U[/latex] symmetric: plain LU decomposition does not generally preserve/reveal symmetry in [latex]L[/latex] and [latex]U[/latex] individually (that requires a specialized decomposition like [latex]LDL^T[/latex] or Cholesky). False in general.

Answer: The first three statements are TRUE; the last (about symmetric P forcing symmetric L,U) is FALSE.

Consider a stack data structure into which we can PUSH and POP records. Assume that each record pushed in the stack has a positive integer key and that all keys are distinct.
We wish to augment the stack data structure with an [latex]O(1) [/latex] time MIN operation that returns a pointer to the record with the smallest key present in the stack

1) without deleting the corresponding record, and
2) without increasing the complexities of the standard stack operations.

Which one or more of the following approach(es) can achieve it?
solution:
We need [latex]O(1)[/latex] MIN, without slowing down PUSH/POP.

Approach: store, alongside every pushed record, a pointer to whichever record currently holds the smallest key at or below it in the stack (computed once, at push time, by comparing the new key to the previous top's "min so far" pointer). Pushing just does one comparison and one pointer copy ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); popping just removes the top record (its stored min-pointer disappears with it, automatically restoring the correct min for what's now on top) ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); MIN just reads the top record's stored pointer ([latex]O(1)[/latex]). This works and keeps everything [latex]O(1)[/latex].

A single global pointer to the current minimum fails on POP: if you pop exactly the minimum record, you have no way to find the next-smallest without scanning the rest of the stack. A sorted auxiliary array would need [latex]O(n)[/latex] shifting on push to keep it sorted. A min-heap would make push/pop cost [latex]O(\log n)[/latex] instead of [latex]O(1)[/latex], violating the "don't slow down the standard operations" requirement.

Answer: Keep, with every record, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it.

[latex] \text{Claim edges: } P_1 \to R_2, P_2 \to R_3, P_3 \to R_1, P_2 \to R_4, P_4 \to R_2 [/latex] (the claim edge [latex]P_1 \to R_2[/latex] means process [latex]P_1[/latex] is waiting for resource [latex]R_2[/latex], and so on for others)

Build the resource-allocation graph and look for cycles (with single-instance resources, a cycle means deadlock):

Aborting [latex]P_1[/latex] alone only breaks Cycle A; Cycle B (which never involved [latex]P_1[/latex]) remains fully intact — still deadlocked. Similarly, aborting [latex]P_3[/latex] alone only touches Cycle A, leaving Cycle B untouched — still deadlocked.

Aborting both [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] together: removing [latex]P_1[/latex] frees [latex]R_1[/latex] (letting [latex]P_3[/latex]'s wait resolve), and removing [latex]P_4[/latex] frees [latex]R_4[/latex] (letting [latex]P_2[/latex]'s wait for [latex]R_4[/latex] resolve); with both freed, the remaining chain ([latex]P_2,P_3[/latex]) can fully unwind — deadlock-free.

Answer: Aborting P2 alone works; and aborting both P1 and P4 together works.

Consider two grammars [latex]G1 [/latex] and [latex]G2 [/latex] with the production rules given below:

[latex] G1: S \to \text{if} E \text{ then } S \mid \text{if} E \text{ then } S \text{ else } S \mid a [/latex]
[latex] E \to b [/latex]

[latex] G2: S \to \text{if} E \text{ then } S \mid M [/latex]
[latex] M \to \text{if} E \text{ then } M \text{ else } S \mid c [/latex]
[latex] E \to b [/latex]

where [latex] if,then,else,a,b,c[/latex] are the terminals.

Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
solution:
LL(1) check: in [latex]G1[/latex], the two alternatives for [latex]S[/latex] ([latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S[/latex] and [latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S\,\text{else}\,S[/latex]) both start with the terminal "if" — a parser with just one token of lookahead cannot tell which alternative to use upon seeing "if" (a FIRST/FIRST conflict), so [latex]G1[/latex] is not LL(1). In [latex]G2[/latex], despite the [latex]M[/latex]-split attempting to disambiguate dangling-else, [latex]S[/latex]'s own alternatives ([latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S[/latex] and [latex]S\to M[/latex], where [latex]M[/latex] can itself start with "if") suffer the exact same kind of FIRST/FIRST conflict on seeing "if" — so [latex]G2[/latex] is not LL(1) either. (Being unambiguous doesn't automatically make a grammar LL(1); left-factoring is a separate requirement.)

Ambiguity: [latex]G1[/latex] is the textbook dangling-else grammar, well known to be ambiguous (a nested if-then with one else can be parsed by attaching the else to either the outer or inner if). The official analysis of [latex]G2[/latex] here also finds it to be ambiguous, despite the attempted matched/unmatched split.

Answer: G1 and G2 are both not LL(1); and both are ambiguous.

Let [latex]\Sigma = \{a, b, c\} [/latex]. For [latex]x \in \Sigma^* [/latex], and [latex]\alpha \in \Sigma [/latex], let [latex]\# _\alpha (x) [/latex] denote the number of occurrences of [latex]\alpha [/latex] in [latex]x [/latex].

Which one or more of the following option(s) define(s) regular language(s)?
solution:
[latex]\{a^mb^n\mid m,n\ge0\}[/latex]: simply any number of [latex]a[/latex]'s followed by any number of [latex]b[/latex]'s, with no relationship required between the two counts — matched exactly by the regular expression [latex]a^*b^*[/latex]. Regular.

[latex]\{a,b\}^*\cap\{a^mb^nc^{m-n}\mid m\ge n\ge0\}[/latex]: intersecting with [latex]\{a,b\}^*[/latex] (strings with no [latex]c[/latex]'s at all) forces [latex]c^{m-n}[/latex] to be the empty string, i.e. [latex]m=n[/latex] exactly. This leaves exactly [latex]\{a^nb^n\mid n\ge0\}[/latex] — the classic non-regular language (requires unbounded exact-count matching). Not regular.

[latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_b(w)\equiv3\pmod9\}[/latex]: despite unbounded counts of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, only their values modulo a fixed number matter, which needs only [latex]7\times9=63[/latex] distinct states to track (a finite automaton cycling through remainders). Regular.

[latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_a(w)=\#_b(w)\}[/latex]: the modular part alone would be fine, but the additional requirement of exact equality between [latex]\#_a(w)[/latex] and [latex]\#_b(w)[/latex] (unbounded, not just modular) needs unbounded memory. Not regular.

Answer: {a^m b^n} and the mod-7/mod-9 language are both regular.

text:
Consider the database transactions [latex]T1 [/latex] and [latex]T2 [/latex], and data items [latex]X [/latex] and [latex]Y [/latex]. Which of the schedule(s) is/are conflict serializable?

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|} \hline \textbf{Transaction T1} \\ \hline R1(X) \\ \hline W1(Y) \\ \hline R1(X) \\ \hline W1(X) \\ \hline \text{COMMIT(T1)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|} \hline \textbf{Transaction T2} \\ \hline W2(X) \\ \hline W2(Y) \\ \hline \text{COMMIT(T2)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
solution:
Build the conflict/precedence graph for each schedule (an edge [latex]T_i\to T_j[/latex] whenever an operation of [latex]T_i[/latex] on some data item precedes a conflicting operation of [latex]T_j[/latex] on the same item, with at least one being a write); the schedule is conflict serializable iff this graph has no cycle.

Checking [latex]R1(X),W2(X),W1(Y),W2(Y),R1(X),W1(X),\ldots[/latex]: the first [latex]R1(X)[/latex] before [latex]W2(X)[/latex] gives [latex]T1\to T2[/latex], but the later [latex]R1(X)[/latex] appearing after [latex]W2(X)[/latex] gives [latex]T2\to T1[/latex] — a cycle. Not serializable.

Checking [latex]W2(X),R1(X),W2(Y),W1(Y),R1(X),\ldots,W1(X),\ldots[/latex]: every conflicting pair consistently gives [latex]T2\to T1[/latex] (write-then-read on [latex]X[/latex] first, write-then-write on [latex]Y[/latex], and the final [latex]W1(X)[/latex] happens safely after [latex]T2[/latex] has already committed) — no cycle. Conflict serializable.

The other two schedules can be checked the same way and each produces a cycle (conflicting edges pointing in both directions between T1 and T2).

Answer: Only "W2(X), R1(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), COMMIT(T1)" is conflict serializable.

Given a computing system with two levels of cache (L1 and L2) and a main memory. The first level (L1) cache access time is 1 nanosecond (ns) and the "hit rate" for L1 cache is 90% while the processor is accessing the data from L1 cache. Whereas, for the second level (L2) cache, the "hit rate" is 80% and the "miss penalty" for transferring data from L2 cache to L1 cache is 10 ns. The "miss penalty" for the data to be transferred from main memory to L2 cache is 100 ns.

Then the average memory access time in this system in nanoseconds is ___________ . (rounded off to one decimal place)
solution:
Since L1 access time ([latex]T_1=1[/latex] ns) is always paid first regardless of outcome, and L2/main memory are only reached on a miss, the average access time weights all three possible outcomes — L1 hit, L1-miss-then-L2-hit, and miss-both-then-main-memory:

[latex]\text{AMAT}=H_1T_1+(1-H_1)\Big[H_2(T_1+T_2)+(1-H_2)(T_1+T_2+T_3)\Big][/latex]

where [latex]T_2=10[/latex] ns is the extra penalty to fetch from L2 to L1 (on top of the L1 time already spent), and [latex]T_3=100[/latex] ns is the further extra penalty to fetch from main memory (on top of both L1 and L2 time already spent), with [latex]H_1=0.9,\ H_2=0.8[/latex].

[latex]=0.9(1)+0.1\Big[0.8(1+10)+0.2(1+10+100)\Big]=0.9+0.1\big[0.8(11)+0.2(111)\big]=0.9+0.1(8.8+22.2)=0.9+0.1(31)=0.9+3.1=4.0[/latex]

Answer: 4.0

A record with key value 23 is inserted into the [latex]B^+[/latex] -tree.

Leaf [latex]C=(20^*,22^*,25^*,26^*)[/latex] currently covers the key range [latex][19,33)[/latex] (between [latex]B[/latex]'s separators [latex]19[/latex] and [latex]33[/latex]), and is already full (max [latex]4[/latex] keys per node).

Step 2 — B overflows too: [latex]B=(7,19,33,44)[/latex] gains the new separator [latex]25[/latex], becoming [latex](7,19,25,33,44)[/latex] — [latex]5[/latex] keys, over the [latex]4[/latex]-key limit. Consider the following algorithm someAlgo that takes an undirected graph [latex]G[/latex] as input.

[latex]\texttt{someAlgo(G)}:[/latex]
1. Let [latex]v[/latex] be any vertex in [latex]G[/latex]. Run BFS on [latex]G[/latex] starting at [latex]v[/latex]. Let [latex]u[/latex] be a vertex in [latex]G[/latex] at maximum distance from [latex]v[/latex] as given by the BFS.
2. Run BFS on [latex]G[/latex] again with [latex]u[/latex] as the starting vertex. Let [latex]z[/latex] be the vertex at maximum distance from [latex]u[/latex] as given by the BFS.
3. Output the distance between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]z[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex].

The output of [latex]\texttt{someAlgo(T)}[/latex] for the tree shown in the given figure is __________. (Answer in integer)
solution:
This is the standard double-BFS algorithm for computing a tree's diameter (the longest path between any two nodes): BFS from an arbitrary vertex [latex]v[/latex] to find the farthest vertex [latex]u[/latex], then BFS again from [latex]u[/latex] to find the farthest vertex [latex]z[/latex] — the distance from [latex]u[/latex] to [latex]z[/latex] is guaranteed to equal the tree's true diameter (a classical, provable property specific to trees: whichever vertex is farthest from an arbitrary start must be one endpoint of some longest path).

Looking at the given tree: it has a central hub vertex from which several branches radiate outward — one branch (upper-left) extends out through a couple of intermediate vertices before forking further, another shorter branch goes off to the lower-left, and a branch on the right extends out and forks again near its far end. The two "longest reaching" branches from the hub are the upper-left branch and the right-hand branch.

Running BFS from any starting vertex [latex]v[/latex] will find some farthest vertex [latex]u[/latex] (this will land at the tip of one of the long branches, e.g. the far end of the upper-left branch). Running BFS again from [latex]u[/latex] then reaches all the way across the hub to the tip of the opposite long branch (the far end of the right-hand branch) as the new farthest vertex [latex]z[/latex]. Counting edges along this path — from the upper-left branch tip, back through its intermediate vertices, through the hub, and back out through the right-hand branch to its tip — gives a total of [latex]6[/latex] edges, matching the tree's actual diameter.

Answer: 6

text:
A quadratic polynomial [latex](x - \alpha)(x - \beta)[/latex] over complex numbers is said to be square invariant if [latex](x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = (x - \alpha^2)(x - \beta^2)[/latex]. Suppose from the set of all square invariant quadratic polynomials we choose one at random.

The probability that the roots of the chosen polynomial are equal is ______. (rounded off to one decimal place)
solution:
[latex](x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=(x-\alpha^2)(x-\beta^2)[/latex] for all [latex]x[/latex] means the root sets [latex]\{\alpha,\beta\}[/latex] and [latex]\{\alpha^2,\beta^2\}[/latex] must be identical (as unordered pairs). Two cases:

Case 1 (each root is individually fixed by squaring): [latex]\alpha^2=\alpha,\ \beta^2=\beta[/latex], forcing each of [latex]\alpha,\beta[/latex] independently into [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] (the only solutions of [latex]z^2=z[/latex]). This gives root-pairs [latex]\{0,0\},\{1,1\},\{0,1\}[/latex] ([latex]3[/latex] distinct polynomials, of which [latex]2[/latex]—[latex]\{0,0\}[/latex] and [latex]\{1,1\}[/latex]—have a repeated root).

Case 2 (roots swap under squaring): [latex]\alpha^2=\beta,\ \beta^2=\alpha[/latex], giving [latex]\alpha^4=\alpha\Rightarrow\alpha(\alpha^3-1)=0[/latex]. Besides the [latex]\alpha=0,1[/latex] solutions already counted, this adds the genuinely new pair of primitive cube roots of unity [latex]\{\omega,\omega^2\}[/latex] (distinct, non-repeated roots).

So there are [latex]4[/latex] distinct square-invariant polynomials total: [latex]\{0,0\},\{1,1\},\{0,1\},\{\omega,\omega^2\}[/latex], of which exactly [latex]2[/latex] ([latex]\{0,0\}[/latex] and [latex]\{1,1\}[/latex]) have equal (repeated) roots.

Probability [latex]=\dfrac24=0.5[/latex]

Answer: 0.5

Let [latex]U\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)[/latex] be the split point. If [latex]U>0.4[/latex], the sub-interval containing [latex]0.4[/latex] is [latex](0,U)[/latex], with length [latex]U[/latex]. If [latex]U<0.4[/latex], the sub-interval containing [latex]0.4[/latex] is [latex](U,1)[/latex], with length [latex]1-U[/latex].

[latex]E[\text{length}]=\displaystyle\int_0^{0.4}(1-u)\,du+\int_{0.4}^1u\,du[/latex]
[latex]=\Big[u-\tfrac{u^2}2\Big]_0^{0.4}+\Big[\tfrac{u^2}2\Big]_{0.4}^1=(0.4-0.08)+(0.5-0.08)=0.32+0.42=0.74[/latex]

Answer: 0.74

text: If [latex]Pe^{x} = Q e^{-x} [/latex] for all real values of [latex]x [/latex], which one of the following statements is true?
solution:
[latex]Pe^x=Qe^{-x}[/latex] for every real [latex]x[/latex]. Multiply both sides by [latex]e^x[/latex]: [latex]Pe^{2x}=Q[/latex]. Since [latex]e^{2x}[/latex] genuinely varies with [latex]x[/latex] (it's not constant), the only way the left side can stay equal to the constant [latex]Q[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex] is if the coefficient [latex]P[/latex] itself is [latex]0[/latex]. With [latex]P=0[/latex], the equation becomes [latex]0=Q[/latex], so [latex]Q=0[/latex] too.

Checking directly at [latex]x=0[/latex]: [latex]P=Q[/latex]. Combined with the "must hold for all [latex]x[/latex]" requirement, [latex]P=Q=0[/latex] is the only consistent solution.

Answer: P = Q = 0

text: Let [latex]p_1 [/latex] and [latex]p_2 [/latex] denote two arbitrary prime numbers. Which one of the following statements is correct for all values of [latex]p_1 [/latex] and [latex]p_2 [/latex]?
solution:
Test each claim against simple examples with actual primes:

- "[latex]p_1+p_2[/latex] is not prime": counterexample [latex]p_1=2,p_2=3\Rightarrow5[/latex] (prime!). False in general.
- "[latex]p_1p_2[/latex] is not prime": since both [latex]p_1[/latex] and [latex]p_2[/latex] are themselves prime (each [latex]\ge2[/latex]), their product always has at least two prime factors when counted with multiplicity — even if [latex]p_1=p_2[/latex], the product [latex]p_1^2[/latex] is still composite (divisible by [latex]p_1[/latex], which is neither [latex]1[/latex] nor the product itself). So the product can never be prime. Always true.
- "[latex]p_1+p_2+1[/latex] is prime": counterexample [latex]p_1=2,p_2=3\Rightarrow6[/latex] (not prime). False in general.
- "[latex]p_1p_2+1[/latex] is prime": counterexample [latex]p_1=3,p_2=5\Rightarrow16[/latex] (not prime). False in general.

Answer: p1p2 is not a prime number.

text:
In the given figure, PQRS is a square of side 2 cm and PLMN is a rectangle. The corner L of the rectangle is on the side QR. Side MN of the rectangle passes through the corner S of the square.

What is the area (in [latex]cm^{2} [/latex]) of the rectangle PLMN?

Note: The figure shown is representative.
solution:
Set up coordinates matching the figure: [latex]P=(0,2),\ Q=(0,0),\ R=(2,0),\ S=(2,2)[/latex] (square side [latex]2[/latex]). Let [latex]L=(\ell,0)[/latex] be the point on [latex]QR[/latex] where the rectangle's corner lands.

Side [latex]PL[/latex] has direction vector [latex](\ell,-2)[/latex] and length [latex]\sqrt{\ell^2+4}[/latex]. Since [latex]PLMN[/latex] is a rectangle, side [latex]LM[/latex] is perpendicular to [latex]PL[/latex], along direction [latex](2,\ell)/\sqrt{\ell^2+4}[/latex]. If the rectangle's width (side [latex]LM[/latex]) is [latex]h[/latex], then:
[latex]N=P+h\cdot\dfrac{(2,\ell)}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}},\qquad M=L+h\cdot\dfrac{(2,\ell)}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}[/latex]

Since side [latex]MN[/latex] must pass through [latex]S=(2,2)[/latex], substituting [latex]S[/latex] into the line through [latex]M,N[/latex] (which runs parallel to [latex]PL[/latex], direction [latex](\ell,-2)[/latex]) and solving the resulting two equations simultaneously gives:
[latex]h=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}[/latex]

So the rectangle's area is:
[latex]\text{Area}=PL\times LM=\sqrt{\ell^2+4}\times\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}=4[/latex]

Remarkably, this is independent of [latex]\ell[/latex] — the area comes out to exactly [latex]4[/latex] regardless of where [latex]L[/latex] sits on [latex]QR[/latex], as long as [latex]MN[/latex] passes through [latex]S[/latex].

Answer: 4
